Vary means to be different — either across different situations, different things, or different points in time — or to deliberately make something different.

Think of it this way: when something varies, it doesn't stay the same. It shifts. It differs. It changes depending on where you look or when you look.

1. Something changes on its own (no object needed)

Here, vary describes a natural or expected difference — something that shifts based on conditions, context, or from one case to another.

"The temperature varies throughout the day."
(It's cool in the morning, hot in the afternoon, cool again at night.)

"Results vary from person to person."
(Not everyone gets the same result.)

"The price of vegetables varies with the season."
(In summer, prices are low; in winter, they rise.)

"Opinions on this topic vary widely."
(Different people hold very different views.)

In all these cases, no one is causing the variation — it just is that way naturally.

2. Someone deliberately changes something (with an object)

Here, a person intentionally introduces difference — to avoid repetition, to improve something, or to adapt to circumstances.

"You should vary your exercise routine."
(Don't do the same workout every day — mix it up.)

"The chef varied the ingredients based on what was available."
(She changed them deliberately.)

"He varied the speed of the car depending on the road."
(He adjusted it on purpose.)

This use carries a slight sense of wisdom or skill — varying something is usually considered good practice, because it shows adaptability and prevents monotony.
The Important Distinction: What "Vary" Is Really Saying

"Vary" is not just about change — it carries a specific idea: difference across a range or set. This is what separates it from similar words.

  • Change = something moves from one state to another (focus is on the transition).

"The weather changed." → It was sunny; now it's rainy.

  • Differ = two specific things are unlike each other (a comparison between two points).

"His opinion differs from mine."

  • Vary = there is a spread of differences — across time, across people, across situations, or across a group.

"Opinions vary." → Across all people, there is a whole range of views, not just two.

"Vary" is the right word when you want to highlight that there is no single fixed answer or state — it depends, it spreads, it ranges.

Learning these patterns will let you use and understand "vary" in almost every situation:

"Vary from X to Y" — describes the full range.

"Temperatures vary from −5°C to 40°C across the country."
"Student scores varied from 40 to 98."

"Vary between X and Y" — same idea, slightly more informal.

"The wait time varies between 10 and 45 minutes."

"Vary with something" — it changes depending on that thing.

"Difficulty varies with experience."
(The more experience you have, the less difficult it becomes — or vice versa.)

"The dosage varies with body weight."

"Vary according to something" — same meaning, slightly more formal.

"Procedures vary according to the company's policies."
"The rules vary according to the country."

"Vary in [a quality]" — specifies what aspect is different.

"The apples vary in size and color."
(Some are big, some are small; some are red, some are green.)

"The students vary in their level of preparation."

You'll often see adverbs before or after "vary" to describe the degree of variation. These are very commonly used:

  • vary widely — big differences, a large range

"Salaries vary widely depending on location."

  • vary greatly / considerably / significantly / enormously — also large variation, slightly more formal

"Quality varies considerably between manufacturers."

  • vary slightly / somewhat / a little — small differences

"The two versions vary slightly in design."

You'll hear and read "it varies" constantly. It's a natural, honest answer when something has no single fixed value.

"How long does the process take?"
"It varies. Sometimes 2 days, sometimes 2 weeks."

This phrase acknowledges that there is no one correct answer — the answer depends on the situation.

Knowing these connected words will help you recognize "vary" in its other shapes:

  • varied (adjective) — describes something that has many different types or is not uniform.

"She has a varied diet." (She eats many different types of food.)
"He has a varied career." (He has done many different kinds of work.)

  • variable (adjective) — describes something that tends to change, is not fixed or stable.

"The weather here is variable." (It keeps changing, you can't predict it.)

  • varying (adjective/present participle) — currently changing, or of different amounts.

"Students arrive at varying times." (Some come early, some late.)
"The medicine comes in varying doses."

  • variation (noun) — the fact or amount of being different.

"There is significant variation in test results."
A Few Real-Life Examples Across Contexts

Science: "The melting point of a substance varies with pressure."

Everyday life: "My energy levels vary throughout the day — I'm sharpest in the morning."

Work/advice: "Try to vary the types of questions you ask in an interview."

Education: "Student performance varies depending on the teaching method used."

Health: "Recovery time varies from patient to patient."
Summary (The Whole Word in a Few Lines)

Vary means: to be different across situations, times, people, or things — or to deliberately make something different.

It highlights a range of difference, not just one change. Something that varies has no single fixed value — it shifts and differs based on conditions. When a person varies something, they are intentionally introducing difference, usually to improve or adapt.

The key patterns to remember: vary from X to Y, vary with something, vary according to something, and vary in [a quality]. The key adverbs: widely, greatly, considerably, slightly.
